articles.title: The AUDUSD and NZDUSD are moving higher today helped by risk-on flow and technicals
articles.description: The AUDUSD and NZDUSD are both moving higher to start the North American session, supported by an improving risk-on backdrop and constructive technical developments. U.S. equity futures are pointing to a stronger open, with S&P 500 futures up roughly 21 points and Nasdaq futures ahead by about 252 points. Helping sentiment are reports that discussions are continuing around a possible 10-day cease-fire in the Middle East, along with renewed optimism that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen to normal shipping traffic. Those headlines have encouraged investors to move back toward risk-sensitive assets, providing a tailwind for both the Australian and New Zealand dollars. For the AUDUSD, the technical picture has also shifted more favorably for buyers. The pair found willing buyers on Friday and again during today's Asian session within a key swing area between 0.6962 and 0.6978. That support zone once again proved its importance, allowing buyers to define their risk against the lower end of the range and begin another move higher. The buying interest gained momentum after the pair broke above its 100-hour moving average and then successfully retested that moving average, currently near 0.6988. Holding that level as support gave buyers greater confidence to extend the rally, with the price reaching a session high near 0.7014 before easing modestly. Even with the slight pullback, the pair remains comfortably above the 100-hour moving average, keeping the near-term bias tilted in favor of the bulls. For buyers to maintain control, the price needs to remain above the 100-hour moving average. A move back below that level would weaken the bullish outlook and shift the focus back toward the sellers, with the rising 200-hour moving average at 0.6962 becoming the next logical downside target. On the topside, a break above today's high and last week's high near 0.7021 would strengthen the bullish case and expose the 100-day moving average at 0.7058. That level is particularly noteworthy because the pair has not traded above its 100-day moving average since June 15, making it an important technical hurdle that could attract additional buying if broken. ﻿﻿ The NZDUSD has displayed even stronger upside momentum over the past several weeks. Since establishing a low on June 26, the pair has consistently carved out a series of higher highs and higher lows, reinforcing the positive technical trend. After reaching a high of 0.5862 last Wednesday, the pair entered a healthy corrective phase that allowed the rising 100-hour moving average to catch up with price. That moving average was tested during early Asian trading today, and buyers once again stepped in aggressively. The successful defense of the 100-hour moving average gave traders another opportunity to define their risk and helped launch the latest push higher, forcing short-term sellers onto the defensive. However, the rally has now run into an important area of resistance. Today's high stalled just below last week's high and the June 15 high, both clustered around the 0.5862 level. That price now represents the key ceiling for buyers. If the pair can break above 0.5862 and sustain trading above that level, it would signal another bullish breakout and increase the likelihood of an extension higher. Until then, buyers still have work to do. On the downside, the first line of defense remains the rising 100-hour moving average, currently near 0.5835. As long as the price stays above that support, buyers retain the near-term technical advantage. A move below the moving average, however, would suggest upside momentum is fading and could trigger a deeper corrective move before the broader uptrend resumes. ﻿ This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

articles.title: HLB Fails in Third FDA Bid—Can It Rebuild Shattered Market Trust?
articles.description: HLB’s liver cancer drug rivoceranib, which the company has developed for more than two decades, has once again failed to clear the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s approval hurdle on its third attempt. With HLB's liver cancer drug "riboseranib" failing to meet the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's third challenge due to HLB's manufacturing facility, the FDA's inspection results have been classified as "Voluntary Improvement Recommendation Measures (VAI)" and rekindled the challenge. / ChatGPT As in the previous reviews, the setback was not attributed to clinical trial results but to manufacturing and quality-control issues involving HLB’s Chinese partner, Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals. HLB has since begun preparing for another regulatory attempt, arguing that the principal issue cited by the FDA has now been resolved as it seeks to restore corporate credibility. According to industry sources, Elevar Therapeutics, HLB’s U.S. subsidiary, recently received an inspection closeout letter from Hengrui concerning the manufacturing facility responsible for producing rivoceranib’s active pharmaceutical ingredient. The FDA classified the inspection outcome as “Voluntary Action Indicated,” or VAI, after determining that the facility was generally operating in compliance with current Good Manufacturing Practice standards. A VAI classification means that inspectors identified conditions requiring improvement but concluded that immediate official regulatory action, such as a warning letter or import restrictions, was not warranted. It carries a lower regulatory risk than an “Official Action Indicated,” or OAI, classification, which is issued when significant violations are found. HLB has emphasized that the closeout letter reportedly states that the VAI classification should not negatively affect pending drug applications associated with the facility. Based on this language, the company believes that the API manufacturing issue cited as a direct cause of its third Complete Response Letter has effectively been addressed. The FDA previously rejected HLB’s application for the rivoceranib-camrelizumab combination as a first-line treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma. It was the third CRL issued for the application, following earlier rejections in 2024 and 2025. Reuters also reported that the latest rejection stemmed from deficiencies at a manufacturing facility linked to the rivoceranib application. Once again, the approval process was derailed by manufacturing and quality-management problems rather than concerns over clinical efficacy or newly identified safety risks. HLB has been seeking approval to use rivoceranib in combination with Hengrui’s immuno-oncology drug camrelizumab as a first-line treatment for patients with unresectable or metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma. Rivoceranib is a targeted anticancer drug that inhibits the formation of blood vessels supplying nutrients to tumor cells. HLB and Elevar are responsible for global development and the U.S. approval process, but production of rivoceranib’s API and camrelizumab depends on Hengrui’s manufacturing facilities in China. HLB maintains that the VAI closeout represents an important turning point that could allow the company to prepare for a fourth approval attempt. Should the FDA determine that compulsory regulatory action against the API facility is unnecessary, the possibility that the facility’s inspection outcome will continue to block approval for an extended period has at least diminished. However, industry observers caution that it is premature to conclude, as HLB has suggested, that the core issues behind the CRL have been completely resolved. A VAI is simply a classification of a manufacturing-facility inspection. It does not mean that the FDA has withdrawn the CRL or formally resumed reviewing the drug application. The actual approval schedule will depend on whether the FDA considers Hengrui’s follow-up corrective measures sufficient and whether it requests additional documentation or another on-site inspection during the resubmission process. Uncertainty also remains over the finished-drug manufacturing facility. Hengrui plans to submit a formal response and a corrective and preventive action, or CAPA, plan addressing observations listed in a Form 483 issued during the FDA’s inspection of the finished-product manufacturing site. A Form 483 is issued by FDA investigators when they identify potential regulatory violations or conditions requiring improvement during an on-site inspection. It remains unclear whether the FDA will accept Hengrui’s CAPA plan through a document review, request further corrective measures or conduct another on-site inspection. HLB has also acknowledged that the FDA’s assessment of the finished-drug facility remains pending, separately from the VAI closeout of the API facility. In addition to the Type A meeting it had initially planned to request, HLB intends to submit an expedited formal inquiry to the FDA. A Type A meeting is an official meeting requested to resolve major regulatory issues, particularly when the review of a new drug application has been suspended or significantly delayed. HLB plans to ask the FDA to clarify whether the causes of the CRL have been sufficiently addressed and to confirm the procedures required for resubmission or the resumption of the review. There remains a possibility that HLB could secure a relatively rapid resubmission pathway through discussions with the FDA. According to the company, the FDA has completed its review of corrective measures involving the camrelizumab manufacturing facility cited in an earlier CRL, while the rivoceranib API facility has now received a VAI closeout. The company also argues that the clinical value of the treatment itself remains intact. The combination improved overall survival and progression-free survival compared with sorafenib, an existing standard treatment. It has already been approved and is being used as a first-line liver cancer treatment in China. Based on publicly available information, the FDA has not cited the combination’s clinical efficacy or any new safety concern as a reason for issuing the CRLs. Manufacturing quality, however, cannot be separated from clinical data in the drug approval process. The efficacy and safety demonstrated in clinical trials must be consistently reproduced in every commercially manufactured batch. Even when clinical results are strong, approval can be denied if any aspect of API or finished-product manufacturing—including production processes, testing methods, contamination controls, data integrity or quality-assurance systems—fails to meet regulatory standards. Another concern is that the facility at issue is believed to be part of Hengrui’s manufacturing complex in Lianyungang, Jiangsu Province. Multiple manufacturing facilities at the complex have reportedly been cited by the FDA over the past several years. In 2024, one formulation plant received an OAI classification and was subsequently issued a warning letter over problems involving data management and the operation of sterile production areas. Several observations were also reported at another plant in the same area. Although the API facility involved in the latest inspection is separate from the previously cited plants, repeated quality-related problems within the same manufacturing complex have raised broader questions about Hengrui’s overall quality-management system. HLB’s greatest challenge may now be the loss of market confidence rather than the delay in the approval timeline. After the first and second CRLs, the company stressed that the issues were manufacturing or administrative matters rather than clinical deficiencies and could be sufficiently corrected. The emergence of another manufacturing-facility issue during the third review, however, has made it more difficult to characterize the repeated approval failures as isolated and unforeseeable incidents. The three CRLs have also raised questions about how accurately HLB assessed and managed the quality risks associated with Hengrui’s manufacturing facilities. Even when problems arise at a partner’s plant, the applicant bears ultimate responsibility for the FDA submission. Should HLB and Elevar have failed to receive sufficient information concerning inspection progress, the possibility of a Form 483 or other quality-control risks, it would suggest weaknesses in their information-sharing system with Hengrui. Conversely, if HLB was aware of the manufacturing risks but continued to communicate an overly optimistic view of the approval prospects and timeline, questions may be raised about the appropriateness of its market communications. The sharp decline in the share prices of HLB and other publicly listed affiliates immediately after the third CRL announcement reflects investors’ perception that the matter involved not merely another approval delay, but broader concerns about the company’s regulatory capabilities and the reliability of its disclosures. There are precedents in which South Korean companies have ultimately obtained FDA approval after receiving repeated CRLs. Hugel received two CRLs for its botulinum toxin product Letybo before winning approval on its third attempt. The company strengthened its manufacturing and quality-management systems, underwent a reinspection and successfully entered the U.S. market. HLB, however, faces greater uncertainty than Hugel did. Hugel won approval during its third review, whereas all three of HLB’s applications have ended in CRLs. Hugel was also able to make improvements directly at its own manufacturing facility. HLB, by contrast, relies on Hengrui for the production of both its core API and the combination drug. This means HLB cannot fully control the speed of facility improvements, the schedule for responding to the FDA or the sharing of inspection-related information. Competition in the U.S. first-line liver cancer treatment market is also intensifying as HLB’s approval is delayed. Roche’s atezolizumab-bevacizumab combination and AstraZeneca’s durvalumab-tremelimumab combination are already established in the market. Even if the rivoceranib combination is eventually approved, it will face the disadvantages of a late entrant in terms of physicians’ prescribing experience, insurance coverage, distribution networks and marketing. “The VAI classification is positive in that one of the direct obstacles behind the third CRL appears to have been removed, as HLB has argued,” an industry official said. “However, it should be viewed more as the restoration of a starting point in the approval process. Formal confirmation from the FDA that the CRL issues have been resolved, acceptance of the CAPA plan for the finished-drug facility and the establishment of a concrete resubmission schedule are all still required.” simalo@chosunbiz.com
